passage:
12 March, 1:40 a.m.
Can't sleep. Sid sent good morning at 6, a voice note at lunch, a poem at 9, and he's still typing. Eight days since the library canteen and he says the universe planned it, that he's been waiting for me his whole life. Nobody has ever said anything like that to me. I feel seen, properly seen, for the first time ever.
Irawati asked tonight what Sid's family is like, what exactly he studies. I didn't know. I laughed it off, but it's sitting in my chest now. How can I feel like I know him completely when I couldn't answer two easy questions?
He wants to meet my parents next week. Part of me is floating. Part of me wants to say, can we just have coffee a few more times first?
I'm going to try that line tomorrow and see how he takes it.
Jahnavi

qa.q: How many days had passed since the library canteen?
qa.a: Eight days had passed since the library canteen.

qa.q: How is Jahnavi feeling about Sid's attention?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels thrilled and seen, almost floating, but also uneasy, because two easy questions about Sid had no answer.

qa.q: What small step could help Jahnavi now?
qa.a: Asking for a few more coffees before meeting parents slows the pace, and how Sid takes that gentle request will show a lot about him.

qa.q: How does Irawati seem to see the romance?
qa.a: Irawati seems caring but curious, asking simple questions about Sid's family and studies that gently test how well Jahnavi really knows him.

grounding: Shows a young adult swept up by constant messages and talk of destiny, feeling seen yet unable to answer basic questions about the person.

subtype: A friend noticing a too-fast bond [Observer]
passage: Every evening for two years, Jagdish and Pankaj had played cricket on the dry field behind the Hanuman temple in their village. This week Pankaj's spot at the crease stayed empty. On Thursday Jagdish found him outside the tea stall, phone glued to his ear. "Megha says we think exactly alike," Pankaj said when he hung up, eyes shining. "She wants me to call every hour. Bhai, it's only been a week and I already know." He had skipped his cousin's engagement, and the bus to exam coaching too. Jagdish felt the urge to say, "You've gone mad," and swallowed it. Instead he sat down on the bench. "You look happy. I've also noticed you've dropped cricket, coaching, everything, in one week. That's a lot, na?" Pankaj frowned, then shrugged. Jagdish stood up. "Match is at five tomorrow. Your bat's in my shed, whenever."

qa.q: Where did Jagdish and Pankaj play cricket every evening?
qa.a: They played on the dry field behind the Hanuman temple in their village.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when Pankaj said he already knew after a week?
qa.a: Jagdish felt worried and frustrated, tempted to say Pankaj had gone mad, but he held it back so as not to shame his friend.

qa.q: Which choice of Jagdish's worked, and why?
qa.a: He named what he saw without judging and left the door open with the bat in his shed, so Pankaj can come back without feeling scolded.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see Jagdish's comment?
qa.a: Pankaj may feel a little defensive, as his frown and shrug suggest, but the calm words give him something to think about without a fight.

grounding: Shows a friend who notices someone drop cricket, coaching and family plans for a week-old partner, names it gently and stays available.

passage:
Counselling note, college wellbeing centre, Tuesday.
Parveen, second year, came in for a follow-up. Three weeks ago she told me that Chinmay, whom she met at a debate meet, wanted to "make it official" after four days and was calling late every night. Today she described what she has tried since. She told him she likes him and wants to go slower. She kept her Saturday badminton with her hostel friends and her weekly call home. She said she is watching how he takes a gentle no.
His reaction, as she reports it: at first he went quiet for a day, then said he understood and asked if Sunday lunch still worked. Parveen laughed as she told me this, and her shoulders looked less raised than at our first meeting. She says she still feels drawn to him but no longer rushed.
Plan: she will keep her routines. Door open if anything changes.

qa.q: What did Parveen keep doing on Saturdays?
qa.a: She kept her Saturday badminton with her hostel friends.

qa.q: How does Parveen feel about Chinmay now?
qa.a: Parveen still feels drawn to Chinmay but no longer rushed; her laugh and less raised shoulders suggest she feels more at ease.

qa.q: What makes Parveen's approach a useful test?
qa.a: By asking for time and keeping friends and routines, Parveen can see how Chinmay handles a gentle no; staying warm, as he did after a day, is a good sign.

qa.q: How might Chinmay experience being asked to slow down?
qa.a: Chinmay might feel a sting of rejection at first, as his quiet day suggests, but asking about Sunday lunch shows he can stay warm when the pace changes.

grounding: Shows a young adult asking for time, keeping friends and routines, and watching how the other person handles a gentle no.

passage: The power went out in the flat at eight, just as Vandana was plating the rajma Amandeep had once called "the best thing I've ever eaten". That was in March, when he sent flowers to her office every Friday and said he'd never met anyone so bright. Now it was November. By candlelight she went over her day: she had ironed his shirts, left her book club early, and not mentioned her promotion, because last time he'd called it showing off. He came in, glanced at the plate, and said the rajma was cold. "The power..." she began. He was already on his phone. Vandana sat in the dark kitchen, scrolling back to their March messages, the hearts, the "my queen". If she just tried harder, surely that man would come back. Then she noticed she had stopped telling her sister anything, and she dialled her number.

qa.q: What had Amandeep once called the rajma?
qa.a: He had once called it the best thing he'd ever eaten.

qa.q: Why was Vandana trying so hard as she went over her day?
qa.a: Vandana felt anxious and desperate to earn back the March warmth, hoping that if she tried harder the old Amandeep would return.

qa.q: What step does Vandana take at the end, and why might it help?
qa.a: She dials her sister after noticing she had stopped telling her anything; reconnecting with someone outside the relationship can help her see the pattern clearly.

qa.q: How might Vandana's sister see the change from March to November?
qa.a: Her sister may have noticed Vandana growing quieter and busier pleasing Amandeep, and may feel both relieved and concerned when the call finally comes.

grounding: Shows a flood of early attention shrinking into criticism and absence, with the receiver working hard to win back the early warmth.

passage: In the apartment lift in Kolkata, Deepika read Arnab's text again: "Can't come Saturday, it's my Dida's eightieth." Her dance recital was on Saturday. She had wanted him in the front row since Class 6. Her thumbs moved fast. "It's fine. I guess I'm just not important. After I sat through your whole football final in the rain." She hit send before she could stop. Three dots appeared, vanished, appeared. "Ok ok I'll come for the first half, I'll tell Dida I'm late." Deepika should have felt happy. Instead her stomach twisted. She pictured Arnab's grandmother cutting the cake with one chair empty. What she had really meant was, I'm nervous and I want you there. She deleted the draft she'd started and typed: "Sorry, that was unfair. Go to Dida's. Can you video-call me before I go on?"

qa.q: Why couldn't Arnab come on Saturday?
qa.a: It was his Dida's eightieth birthday.

qa.q: Why did Deepika's stomach twist when Arnab gave in?
qa.a: Deepika felt guilty, picturing his grandmother's empty chair, and saw that she had used her hurt as a lever instead of saying she was nervous.

qa.q: What did Deepika's final message get right?
qa.a: She apologised and asked for something fair, a video call, instead of using guilt to make Arnab miss his Dida's birthday.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt reading that he was making her feel unimportant?
qa.a: Arnab likely felt torn and guilty, caught between his grandmother and his friend, which is why the dots kept appearing and vanishing.

grounding: Shows a teenager using hurt and reminders of past favours to make a friend give in, then turning it into an honest request.

passage: In the electronics lab, Afreen had just packed her bag when Ojas slumped against the bench. "So you're leaving. Cool. I'll just stay till midnight alone, like always." Afreen froze. This was the third evening this week. On Monday she had written his half of the report; on Wednesday she had skipped her sister's call to solder his board. Each time she said no, he sighed, went silent, and brought up how he'd lent her notes in first year. Her chest tightened now the same way. She asked herself a question she'd heard from the hostel counsellor: had she actually done something wrong? She hadn't. The circuit was his task, and she had finished hers. "I'm going, Ojas," she said, voice shaky. "I can look at your board with you tomorrow at ten, for an hour." He rolled his eyes. She walked out anyway, heart pounding, and then lighter.

qa.q: What had Afreen done for Ojas on Monday?
qa.a: On Monday she had written his half of the report.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when Ojas slumped against the bench?
qa.a: Afreen felt a familiar guilt, her chest tightening, as if his mood were her responsibility to fix.

qa.q: What question helped Afreen, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether she had actually done something wrong showed her the guilt was working as a lever, since the circuit was Ojas's task and hers was finished.

qa.q: How might Ojas see Afreen's offer of an hour tomorrow?
qa.a: Ojas seems annoyed, rolling his eyes because the old pressure no longer works; later he may see the hour as fair help.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps giving in to sighs, sulking and reminders of past favours, and begins to test whether the guilt is real.

passage:
Sunday: Urmila told Farhan she wouldn't run the weekend chaat stall with him next season; her new job had Saturday shifts. Farhan stared at the tawa. "After I taught you everything. Fine. I'll manage. Somehow." Urmila went home with her stomach in knots and almost texted, "Forget it, I'll do it."
Tuesday: At the bus stop she made two columns in her notes. Did I break a promise? No, they had agreed on one season. Did I hurt him by lying or being careless? No. Is he sad? Yes. Is that the same as me doing wrong? She sat with that until her bus came.
Friday: She met him at the stall before opening. "I'm grateful you taught me, and I'll miss this. My answer is still no. My cousin Irfan wants weekend work; can I send him over?" Farhan was quiet, then nodded. Urmila walked away sad, but not guilty.

qa.q: What did Urmila's new job have that clashed with the stall?
qa.a: Her new job had Saturday shifts.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel after Farhan's reply on Sunday?
qa.a: Urmila felt guilty, with her stomach in knots, so pressured that she almost texted to take the stall back.

qa.q: How did Urmila's two columns help her decide?
qa.a: They separated real wrongs, such as breaking a promise, from Farhan's sadness, so she could keep her decision while still showing care in words.

qa.q: What might Farhan feel when Urmila offers her cousin Irfan?
qa.a: Farhan may still feel disappointed, but the thanks and the offer show care, which may ease his hurt and explain his nod.

grounding: Shows a person checking whether they actually wronged someone, then keeping the decision while showing care, because compassion is not compliance.

passage:
Thursday night
Today Chetan said in front of everyone that on Monday in art period I called his drawing "baby scribbles". And I said, "I never said that. You're way too sensitive, seriously." Everyone laughed, and he went red and stared at his desk.
But I did say it. I remember exactly. I was annoyed because Ma'am praised his drawing and not mine.
Why did I lie so fast? I think because saying yes, I said it, felt like admitting I'm a mean person, and I'm not. I'm the one who always stands up for people. Or I thought I was.
The worst part was his face, like he was checking whether he'd made it all up.
Tomorrow before assembly I'll tell Chetan, just him: you didn't imagine it, I said it, I'm sorry. My hands are sweaty even writing that.
Nirmala

qa.q: What had Nirmala called Chetan's drawing on Monday?
qa.a: Nirmala called his drawing “baby scribbles” in art period.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala deny saying it?
qa.a: Nirmala felt ashamed and defensive; admitting it felt like admitting to being a mean person, which clashed with being the one who stands up for people.

qa.q: What makes Nirmala's plan for tomorrow a good repair?
qa.a: Telling Chetan privately that he didn't imagine it restores his trust in his own memory and owns the fault plainly.

qa.q: What was it like for Chetan to be told he was too sensitive?
qa.a: Chetan went red and stared at his desk, and seemed to wonder whether he had made it all up, so the denial hurt twice.

grounding: Shows a teenager denying a hurtful remark and calling the other too sensitive to avoid blame, driven by a self-image that could not bear the truth.

passage:
Dear Masi,
Thank you for yesterday's call. I've been thinking about it all day.
For weeks I thought I was going mad. When Harish and the others put my old photo on the class group with that caption and everyone laughed, I cried in the washroom. The next day Harish said, "What photo? Nobody posted anything, you always twist things." The post was gone. By the end of the week even I wasn't sure. Maybe I was overreacting. Maybe it was a joke.
Then you asked me one question: what did you feel when you saw it? And I knew. I felt humiliated. That part didn't need proof.
You said I wasn't imagining it and it wasn't my fault, and before we hung up you helped me write to Ms Rao. She replied last night that she'll speak to the class and the counsellor today.
I feel steadier.
Love,
Anjali

qa.q: What did Harish say the next day?
qa.a: Harish said, “What photo? Nobody posted anything, you always twist things.”

qa.q: How did Anjali feel by the end of that week?
qa.a: Anjali felt confused and full of doubt, unsure whether the post had happened or whether it was overreacting to a joke.

qa.q: How did Masi's help work?
qa.a: Masi asked about Anjali's feelings, said it was not imagined and not Anjali's fault, and helped write to Ms Rao during that same call, bringing in someone who could act.

qa.q: What would change if Anjali had not spoken to anyone outside the class?
qa.a: Anjali might have kept doubting the memory, Harish's version could have become the only story, and nobody at school would have stepped in.

grounding: Shows a teenager told that a hurtful post never happened who begins doubting it, until a trusted adult outside the situation restores trust in their own perception.
